name: MathlibAnnex.PluckerBody.normalizedGenerator_mem_of_sphereIsometry
title: A target contraction generator lies in the source body

content.display_title: A target contraction generator lies in the source body
content.one_sentence_role: Transfers membership through two extensions with the same boundary trace.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $m,N\in\mathbb N_0$, put $n=m+1>0$, and give $E=\mathbb R^n$ and $F=\mathbb R^N$ their coordinate sup norms. Let $\lambda_n$ be the fixed coordinate Lebesgue measure on $E$. Let $p,q:E\to\mathbb R$ be continuous real seminorms with specified positive constants $a_p,b_p,a_q,b_q$ such that
$$a_p\|x\|_\infty\le p(x)\le b_p\|x\|_\infty,\qquad a_q\|x\|_\infty\le q(x)\le b_q\|x\|_\infty\quad(x\in E).$$

Both $p$ and $q$ are norms. For each $s\in\{p,q\}$ define the closed unit ball, unit sphere, and real reference volume by
$$K_s=\{x:s(x)\le1\},\qquad\Sigma_s=\{x:s(x)=1\},\qquad v_s=\lambda_n(K_s)\in(0,\infty).$$
The finite measure is read as a real number when used as a scalar.

Let $\mathcal I_{n,N}$ be the finite set of increasing $n$-tuples of distinct rows from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. The minor-coordinate space $\mathbb R^{\mathcal I_{n,N}}$ carries its sup norm. For a linear map $B:E\to F$, put $B_{ij}=(Be_j)_i$ in the standard coordinate basis. Write $\Pi_n(B)$ for its maximal-minor vector and $\mathcal V_p(B),\mathcal V_q(B)$ for its two volume-scaled versions. Their coordinates and scaling are
$$\Pi_n(B)_I=\det(B_{i_a,j})_{a,j=1}^n,\qquad\mathcal V_s(B)=v_s\Pi_n(B)\ (s\in\{p,q\})\quad(I=(i_1<\cdots<i_n)).$$

A $p$-contraction is a linear map $B:E\to F$ satisfying $\|Bz\|_\infty\le p(z)$ for every $z\in E$. Write $\mathcal C_p^N$ for these maps. Write $\mathcal G_p^N$ for the signed generator set and $\mathcal P_p^N$ for its real convex hull, so
$$\mathcal G_p^N=\{\mathcal V_p(B),-\mathcal V_p(B):B\in\mathcal C_p^N\},\qquad\mathcal P_p^N=\operatorname{conv}_{\mathbb R}(\mathcal G_p^N).$$

Let $\Delta:\Sigma_p\to\Sigma_q$ be a bijection preserving chord distances, so
$$q(\Delta(u)-\Delta(v))=p(u-v)\qquad(u,v\in\Sigma_p).$$
Read its radial extension on the reference coordinates:
$$R_\Delta(0)=0,\qquad R_\Delta(x)=p(x)\Delta(x/p(x))\quad(x\ne0).$$
For $x\ne0$, positivity of $p(x)$ makes $x/p(x)\in\Sigma_p$, so this is defined.

Let $A:E\to F$ be a $q$-contraction, meaning $\|Az\|_\infty\le q(z)$ for all $z\in E$. Then its target generator belongs to the source body:
$$\mathcal V_q(A)\in\mathcal P_p^N.$$
content.assumptions: The dimension is $n=m+1>0$. The norms $p,q$ have the stated continuity and positive comparison constants; $\Delta$ is a bijective chord-distance isometry. Here $A$ must be a $q$-contraction. The integration measure remains fixed, and $N$ is any nonnegative integer.
content.conclusion: The positively signed target vector $v_q\Pi_n(A)$ belongs to $\mathcal P_p^N$, regardless of the orientation sign of the radial extension.
content.proof_summary: Extend the boundary contraction, compare its average with a radial average, then use sign symmetry.

proof_steps.text:
**Form the boundary map and extend it.** Let $h(u)=A\Delta(u)$ for $u\in\Sigma_p$. Then
$$\|h(u)-h(v)\|_\infty=\|A(\Delta(u)-\Delta(v))\|_\infty\le q(\Delta(u)-\Delta(v))=p(u-v).$$
The contraction hypothesis and chord isometry supply exactly the input of [the boundary-extension theorem](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Plucker/BoundaryExtension.lean#L95-L109). Choose its single witness $f$. For any $k:E\to F$, write $Dk(x)$ for its Fréchet derivative where it exists and for zero otherwise. Define
$$G_{p,k}(x)=v_p\Pi_n(Dk(x)),\qquad \mathcal A_p(k)=v_p^{-1}\int_{K_p}G_{p,k}(x)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$ The five outputs are
$$\begin{gathered}\|f(x)-f(y)\|_\infty\le p(x-y),\qquad f|_{\Sigma_p}=h,\\Df(x)\in\mathcal C_p^N\ \text{a.e. on }K_p,\qquad G_{p,f}\in L^1(K_p),\qquad\mathcal A_p(f)\in\mathcal P_p^N.\end{gathered}$$

**Compare two extensions only on the boundary.** Put $H=A\circ R_\Delta$. For every $u\in\Sigma_p$,
$$f(u)=h(u)=A\Delta(u)=A(R_\Delta(u))=H(u).$$
The equality $R_\Delta(u)=\Delta(u)$ holds because $p(u)=1$. The maps may differ away from the boundary. Let $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ denote the operator norm for the two coordinate sup norms. Their global reference-norm estimates are
$$\begin{aligned}\|f(x)-f(y)\|_\infty&\le b_p\|x-y\|_\infty,\\
\|H(x)-H(y)\|_\infty&\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\frac{3b_p}{a_q}\|x-y\|_\infty.\end{aligned}$$
For the second, use linearity of $A$ and the radial $3$-Lipschitz estimate with the comparison constants; it is not a $1$-Lipschitz assertion for the radial extension.

**Transfer the minor integrals and normalize.** For each $I\in\mathcal I_{n,N}$, the boundary comparison gives
$$\int_{K_p}\Pi_n(Df(x))_I\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_{K_p}\Pi_n(DH(x))_I\,d\lambda_n(x).$$
Apply [the boundary-equality theorem for maximal-minor integrals](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/MeasureTheory/Integral/MaximalMinorBoundary.lean#L297-L309) with the continuous seminorm $p$, compact ball $K_p$, positive dimension $n=m+1$, maps $f,H$, and the global Lipschitz bounds of Step 2. Its remaining hypothesis is exactly $f(u)=H(u)$ on $\Sigma_p$, also established in Step 2. This produces the displayed equality for the same row selection $I$.
[Compact-set integrability of derivative generators](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Plucker/Average.lean#L83-L114) applied separately to $f$ and $H$ on $K_p$ justifies their vector integrals. For either $k=f$ or $k=H$,
$$\begin{aligned}(\mathcal A_p(k))_I
&=v_p^{-1}\int_{K_p}v_p\Pi_n(Dk(x))_I\,d\lambda_n(x)\\
&=\int_{K_p}\Pi_n(Dk(x))_I\,d\lambda_n(x).
\end{aligned}$$
The cancellation uses $v_p>0$. Substituting the equal minor integrals yields
$$\mathcal A_p(f)=\mathcal A_p(H).$$
This is [the average comparison from boundary traces](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Plucker/BodyInvariance.lean#L120-L131); it compares the averages, not the functions away from their common boundary.

**Insert the signed radial average and remove its sign.** [The common-sign radial-average theorem](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Plucker/RadialAverage.lean#L331-L363) supplies $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$ and
$$\sigma\mathcal V_q(A)=\mathcal A_p(H)=\mathcal A_p(f)\in\mathcal P_p^N.$$
Read from the known member at the right: Step 1 gives $\mathcal A_p(f)\in\mathcal P_p^N$; Step 3 identifies this vector with $\mathcal A_p(H)$; the radial-average formula identifies it with $\sigma\mathcal V_q(A)$. If $\sigma=1$, this already gives the conclusion. If $\sigma=-1$, [body sign symmetry](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Convex/PluckerBody.lean#L41-L50) applied to $-\mathcal V_q(A)$ gives $\mathcal V_q(A)\in\mathcal P_p^N$.

content.lean_realization_notes: The historical name “normalized generator” refers here to the volume-multiplied vector $v_q\Pi_n(A)$. It is not division by $v_q$.
